title: Congenital and acquired neck masses: branchial anomalies, thyroglossal duct cysts, and nodal metastases

steps.tx: Differential diagnosis of a cervical **mass** is governed by age and anatomical triangles. In children, over 85 percent of masses are inflammatory or congenital anomalies. In adults older than 40 years, an asymptomatic lateral neck mass represents metastatic squamous cell carcinoma from an occult upper aerodigestive tract mucosal primary until proven otherwise. Initial diagnostic evaluation requires fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) and panendoscopy; open incisional biopsy is strictly contraindicated.
steps.say: Neck masses vary by age. In children, 85 percent are benign or congenital. In adults over 40, a persistent lateral neck mass is considered metastatic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. Evaluation requires fine-needle aspiration and endoscopy; incisional biopsy is contraindicated.

steps.tx: Thyroglossal **duct** cyst (TGDC) arises from failure of obliteration of the embryonic thyroid descent pathway from the foramen cecum of the tongue base to the inferior neck. It presents as a painless, smooth, cystic midline mass located below the hyoid bone that elevates with tongue protrusion and swallowing. Definitive cure requires the Sistrunk procedure: en bloc resection of the cyst, the central body of the hyoid bone, and a core of tongue base tissue.
steps.say: Thyroglossal duct cysts result from incomplete obliteration of the thyroid descent tract. They present as midline masses that elevate with tongue protrusion. Surgical cure requires the Sistrunk procedure, which resects the cyst, central hyoid bone, and a tongue base tissue core.

steps.tx: Branchial **cleft** anomalies arise from incomplete involution of embryonic pharyngeal arches. Second branchial cleft anomalies represent 95 percent of cases, typically manifesting as a smooth, fluctuant mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. The fistulous tract ascends between internal and external carotid arteries and terminates in the tonsillar fossa. First branchial anomalies relate to the parotid gland and external auditory canal.
steps.say: Second branchial cleft cysts account for 95 percent of branchial anomalies, presenting along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The tract passes between the internal and external carotid arteries to the tonsillar fossa. Surgical excision requires complete tract removal.

steps.tx: Neck **dissection** classifications standardize regional oncological lymphadenectomy across cervical levels I through VI. Radical neck dissection (RND) removes all nodal levels I-V along with the sternocleidomastoid muscle, internal jugular vein, and spinal accessory nerve. Modified radical neck dissection (MRND) preserves one or more of these non-lymphatic structures. Selective neck dissection resects only nodal levels at greatest risk of occult metastases based on primary tumor location.
steps.say: Cervical lymph node dissections are categorized from levels I through VI. Radical neck dissection removes levels I through V plus the spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid. Modified radical dissections preserve non-lymphatic structures, while selective dissections target specific levels.
